Additionally, 15 U.S.C. 1681i ( a ) requires consumer reporting agencies to conduct a reasonable reinvestigation of disputed information and delete information that can not be verified. 

Further, 15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ) requires consumer reporting agencies to maintain reasonable procedures to assure the maximum possible accuracy of the information contained in consumer reports. 

As a debt collector, IC System is prohibited under 15 U.S.C. 1692e, including 15 U.S.C. 1692e ( 2 ) ( A ), from making any false, deceptive, or misleading representation regarding the character, amount, or legal status of an alleged debt. Additionally, 15 U.S.C. 1692f prohibits the use of unfair or unconscionable means to collect an alleged obligation.

Pursuant to Regulation F, 12 C.F.R. 1006.18 and 1006.22, debt collectors are prohibited from using false, deceptive, misleading, unfair, or unconscionable practices in connection with the collection of a consumer debt. 

To date, IC System has failed to provide competent documentary evidence establishing : That I am legally obligated to pay the alleged {$150.00} balance ; The contractual basis supporting the amount being reported ; A complete itemization demonstrating how the alleged balance was calculated ; Documentation establishing that the information being furnished is complete, accurate, and legally enforceable.

Continued furnishing of information that can not be substantiated through a reasonable investigation may constitute inaccurate credit reporting under the Fair Credit Reporting Act and continues to cause consumer harm.

Immediately cease furnishing this account to XXXX XXXX XXXX, and any other consumer reporting agency. 
Request deletion of every tradeline furnished by IC System concerning this alleged account because the information is disputed and, if it can not be substantiated through a reasonable investigation, should not continue to be reported. 
Provide written documentary proof establishing that IC System has the legal authority to collect this alleged debt. 
Provide written documentary proof establishing that I am legally responsible for the alleged debt. 
Provide a complete itemization explaining how the alleged {$150.00} balance was calculated. 
Provide documentation establishing the accuracy and legal basis of the information currently being furnished to consumer reporting agencies. 
If IC System can not substantiate this alleged debt through competent documentary evidence, immediately cease all collection activity, cease furnishing this account, and request deletion of every tradeline furnished to any consumer reporting agency. 

I reserve all rights afforded to me under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, Regulation F, and all other applicable federal and state consumer protection laws.

On XX/XX/XXXX I filed CFPB complaint XXXX against Security Credit Services LLC demanding five validation documents under FDCPA Section 1692g ( b ) for a reported {$850.00} collection ( their account XXXX, contract XXXX ). This complaint documents what that production proves and what it fatally omits. 

FIRST FACTUAL DEFECT, THE CHAIN OF TITLE THEY ADMITTED IS BROKEN : Security Credit Services produced no executed assignment of any kind. The only assignment instrument in its production, the Negotiation and Assignment block on page 8 of the lease, is blank. It is unsigned by the lessor, undated, and no recourse election is marked. Worse, its response letter dated XX/XX/XXXX, signed by Support Supervisor XXXX XXXX, states that Security Credit Services " purchased the account from XXXX XXXX, XXXX on XX/XX/XXXX. '' XXXX XXXX, XXXX appears nowhere in the documents it produced. The lease names XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX as the contemplated assignee. No document evidences any transfer from XXXX to XXXX XXXX, from XXXX XXXX to XXXX XXXX, or from XXXX XXXX XXXX Security Credit Services. The furnisher 's own narrative now requires a four-entity chain ( XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, Security Credit Services ) for which it has produced XXXX executed links, and the third entity in that chain was never disclosed until this response. A debt collector that can not document its own ownership of an account can not validate it under Section 1692g ( b ), can not truthfully represent its right to collect it under Section 1692e, and can not certify the accuracy of the tradeline it furnishes under FCRA Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ) ( 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ) ).

RELATED DEFECT, THREE DIFFERENT ORIGINAL CREDITORS : The same response identifies the original creditor three different ways. Its XXXX  tradeline reports Original Creditor Name as " No Info. '' The Re : line of its XX/XX/XXXX letter states " Original Creditor : XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. '' The body of the same letter states the account " was originally opened with XXXX  '' One furnisher, one response, three contradictory identifications of the most basic fact about the account. At least two of the three are false representations under Section 1692e, and the " No Info '' field remains a facial Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ) accuracy violation.

SECOND FACTUAL DEFECT, THE AMOUNT : The {$850.00} it reports is wrong on the face of its own production. Its XX/XX/XXXX letter describes the figure as a " principal balance of {$850.00}. '' That characterization is false by the letter 's own next sentence, which states " the total cost of the lease was in the amount of {$820.00} for 12 payments of {$67.00} with a residual payment of {$47.00}. '' The lease 's capitalized cost, the only figure that could be called principal, is {$310.00}. The {$850.00} figure is the full-term lease total INCLUDING the {$47.00} end-of-lease residual purchase option, the price of an ownership option that was never exercised on a lease that defaulted in its first month ( first payment XXXX  XX/XX/XXXX per the XXXX XXXX  ). The lease 's own Section 8 early-termination clause requires a lesser-of calculation that was never performed, and the agreement states three different full-term totals across its own pages ( {$800.00}, {$820.00}, and {$850.00} ). Representing {$850.00} as " principal '' and furnishing it as the balance is a false representation of the character and amount of a debt under FDCPA Section 1692e ( 2 ) ( A ) and an inaccurate balance under FCRA Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ).

THIRD FACTUAL DEFECT, THE SERVICER 'S OWN LEDGER : The XXXX XXXX printout Security Credit Services chose to produce shows the account was written off XX/XX/XXXX as XXXX XXXX XXXX - XXXX  '' with Times Over 30, Over 60, and Over 90 each recorded as XXXX. Their own evidence contradicts the derogatory severity being furnished. 

FOURTH FACTUAL DEFECT, STILL UNCURED : The XXXX  tradeline continues to report Original Creditor Name as " No Info '' even though Security Credit Services ' own production identifies the originator ( XXXX  ) and the named assignee ( XXXX XXXX XXXX ). The furnisher demonstrably possesses the original-creditor information and furnishes a blank field anyway. That is a facial Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ) accuracy violation independent of validation.

'' I demand written confirmation of the date of first delinquency being furnished to each bureau under FCRA Section 623 ( a ) ( 5 ), to confirm the obsolescence clock under Section 605 runs from the true XXXX delinquency and has not been re-aged.

FCRA Section 605 ( c ) ( 15 U.S.C. 1681c ( c ) ) runs the 7-year period from 180 days after the commencement of the delinquency that preceded the charge-off, here on or about XX/XX/XXXX, not from the charge-off date, and there is no " whichever is earlier '' election. '' On chain of title it states " there is no basis in law to substantiate your right to such information, '' citing XXXX v. XXXX, a XXXX XXXX XXXX decision. Whatever the outer limits of Section 1692g validation, a furnisher responding to a dispute about WHO OWNS the account can not refuse to examine its own acquisition documents. Its licensure is separately before the Florida Office of Financial Regulation under Fla. Stat. 559.553, where " we deny the allegation '' is not proof.

XXXX ), the Section 1681s-2 ( b ) reasonable-investigation duty squarely covers objectively and readily verifiable facts : whether an executed assignment to Security Credit Services exists , what the contract 's own termination formula yields, and who the original creditor is. Every one of those is answerable from documents Security Credit Services itself selected and produced.

Stat. 559.72 ( 9 ). Each federal violation above additionally serves as a per se predicate under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, Fla. Stat. 501.201 et seq. Security Credit Services ' Florida licensure posture is separately before the Florida Office of Financial Regulation under Fla. Stat. 559.553.

I am a XXXX senior citizen in Texas, suffering from XXXX illnesses. My husband ( XXXX ) is also severely ill. We survive solely on low Social Security income and are legally judgment-proof in Texas. This collection action by Resurgent Capital Services and LVNV Funding is causing severe emotional distress, forcing us to delay critical medical procedures due to financial and physical stress. I have clearly indicated we are judgment proof and dont even have enough money monthly to survive all of our needs. 

The collection attempts stem from an alleged old XXXX XXXX debt ( Origination : XX/XX/XXXX ). XXXX XXXX completely ceased operations and legal existence by XX/XX/XXXX when it was acquired by XXXX XXXX. Because XXXX ceased to exist in XX/XX/XXXX, any alleged contract being used by Resurgent Capital Services and LVNV Funding LLC was cancelled, altered or rewritten by XXXX XXXX  without reference to XXXX XXXX and some provisions were actually changed in new contracts. 

I contacted free Senior Legal Aid provided in Texas as to addressing my rights while addressing this issue. If one looks online for information, it is well known and documented that many errors were made in the transfer of the XXXX debts to XXXX, resulting in complaints and lawsuits by people disputing the validity of debts. I was contacted in XXXX regarding this debt by an independent Attorneys Office and supplied them with my dispute of the debt. I assumed the issue had been resolved because I did not receive any further contact after this situation and heard nothing further until Resurgent and LVNV funding contacted me in XXXX of XXXX. In this process, Resurgent has indicated that they got chain of title information from XXXX XXXX, who I have had no dealings with at all. 

I indicated the reasons why I was disputing the debt to Resurgent and LVNV Funding and labeled my letter as a notice to cease communication unless they were providing some contract signed by me so that I could see what they were viewing from XXXX XXXX or bills of transfer and sale establishing verifiable transfers of the debt from XXXX XXXX to all of the parties mentioned herein ending with Resurgent Capital Services or LVNV Funding since some lawsuits cited online also say sale of some accounts were to only one of the two entities and not the final entity addressing the collection and claiming to be the owner OR I said I would allow the contact if they were indicating they intend to sue me. 
I did this cease communication notice boldly at the top of two successive letters very clearly, sent the letters via certified mail, and the most recent follow up from Resurgent Capital Services and LVNV Funding simply still provides no documented chain of title and only a simple half page statement of claimed dates regarding the account and includes a statement that says This account summary has been prepared by Resurgent Capital Services on behalf of LVNV Funding LLC. It is not a credit card or other account statement from the original creditor. 

In the most recent communication from them, they say, instead of giving me the full chain of title information, that they are disputing my dispute of the debt because I am not providing sufficient information to support my claim that there is likely an error or inaccuracy in the files of information they have. This seems somewhat pompous to me when they wont even show me the documented information that they are basing their hard-core press on me with. And quite frankly, I would ask for full discovery on this information if I am taken to court. 
I have been told that Resurgent and LVNV are violating 15 U.S.C. 1692g and 15 U.S.C. 1692e by refusing to provide a complete, unbroken chain of title or legal assignment proving they own this specific account. They refuse to clarify if they intend to sue, although they allude to the possibility, and yet they refuse to stop communicating. I have explicitly instructed them in writing to cease communication unless providing proof or notice of a lawsuit, but they continue to mail me incomplete data briefs while demanding that I " substantiate '' why I do not owe them money. 
All of this also seems vindictive and pointless since I have delineated that I am considered judgment proof in Texas with no assets or cash and only limited Social Security and life-threatening illness for both I and my husband. I understand they might get lucky and get a judgment but there would be nothing to collect and neither of us are able to work any longer. And, if sued, I would go to court if I am not in the hospital at the time and state my case as best I can. 

This feels like an attempt at harassment of an elderly sick person because the debt collector thinks that they at least can coerce some payment because the person is upset and might pay something to escape the ongoing trauma and threats of a lawsuit. People like me can not afford an attorney, which is why I called the free Senior Legal Aid.

After speaking with Senior Legal Aid, I now demand that Resurgent and LVNV Funding immediately cease all communication, close this account, and stop reporting incomplete information regarding this unverified, disputed debt.

This complaint concerns multiple Navy Federal Credit Union accounts that continue appearing on my credit reports as charge-offs, collection accounts, and accounts with extensive late payment histories. I discovered these accounts after reviewing my consumer reports and immediately disputed them because I did not recognize them. After discovering the accounts, I filed an FTC Identity Theft Report and submitted disputes to the credit bureaus and Navy Federal Credit Union. Despite these actions, the accounts continue to be reported. According to the prior CFPB complaint records, I repeatedly informed Navy Federal Credit Union that I do not own these accounts and that they are the result of identity theft. 

The accounts in question are reported with significant derogatory histories, including charge-offs, collections, and numerous late payments. The continued reporting of these accounts falsely suggests that I opened, used, and defaulted on Navy Federal Credit Union accounts when I did not. These inaccurate reports have significantly lowered my credit scores, damaged my financial standing, and created obstacles when applying for credit and other financial products. 

I filed an FTC Identity Theft Report because I believe these accounts were opened or used without my authorization. Once an FTC Identity Theft Report is filed and submitted, federal law provides protections to consumers who are victims of identity theft. I expected Navy Federal Credit Union to review my identity theft claim, investigate the disputed accounts, and provide documentation proving that I personally opened and authorized the accounts. Instead, Navy Federal Credit Union continued reporting the accounts and associated derogatory information. 

According to Navy Federal Credit Union 's prior response, the company relied primarily on account history and payment activity to conclude that the accounts belonged to me. However, payment history does not establish ownership. The existence of payments on an account does not prove who opened the account, who authorized the account, or who benefited from the account. Identity theft frequently involves accounts that show payment activity before becoming delinquent. The key issue is not whether payments occurred. The key issue is whether I personally opened and authorized the accounts. 

I repeatedly requested documentation proving ownership. Specifically, I requested signed credit applications, original account opening records, identity verification records, signature records, account origination documentation, and records showing how Navy Federal Credit Union verified the identity of the person who opened the accounts. These are the types of records that would establish ownership. Despite my requests, Navy Federal Credit Union did not provide documentation proving that I personally opened the disputed accounts. The prior CFPB complaint specifically noted that billing statements and account summaries do not establish that a consumer opened or authorized an account. 

Instead of providing original account documentation, Navy Federal Credit Union relied on account histories and payment records. Those records may demonstrate activity on an account, but they do not prove ownership. They do not establish that I opened the accounts, authorized the accounts, received the proceeds, or personally benefited from the accounts. As noted in my prior disputes, I dispute ownership itself, not merely the payment history associated with the accounts.

I also requested a complete Method of Verification regarding the disputed accounts. I asked Navy Federal Credit Union to explain how the accounts were verified, what systems were used, whether the review was manual or automated, who conducted the review, and what documents were examined during the investigation. According to the prior complaint documentation, Navy Federal Credit Union failed to provide a meaningful verification methodology, audit trail, explanation of how identity theft was ruled out, or confirmation of human review. 

This failure is significant because consumers have the right to understand how disputed information was investigated. A generic statement that an account belongs to a consumer is not sufficient. If Navy Federal Credit Union truly investigated my identity theft claim, it should be able to identify the records reviewed, the investigative steps taken, and the evidence used to determine that the accounts belong to me. To date, I have not received that information. 

Another major issue involves Navy Federal Credit Union 's continued reporting of the accounts after receiving my FTC Identity Theft Report. Under federal law, identity theft claims trigger specific obligations. Once a consumer provides an identity theft report and disputes ownership of an account, the furnisher and consumer reporting agencies are required to take appropriate action. My prior complaint specifically noted that Navy Federal Credit Union continued reporting the disputed accounts despite receiving notice of identity theft. 

I believe Navy Federal Credit Union failed to conduct a proper identity theft investigation. A proper investigation should include reviewing original account opening records, examining identity verification procedures, reviewing application information, reviewing signatures, analyzing IP address information when available, examining device information, reviewing contact information used at account opening, and determining whether the person who opened the accounts can be positively linked to me. Based on the documentation provided thus far, it does not appear that Navy Federal Credit Union performed this type of investigation. 

I am also concerned that Navy Federal Credit Union improperly shifted the burden of proof back onto me. I filed an FTC Identity Theft Report, submitted disputes, and provided supporting information. After receiving these materials, the burden shifted to Navy Federal Credit Union to demonstrate that the accounts belong to me. Instead, the company continued to request additional information while failing to provide the documentation necessary to prove ownership. The prior complaint specifically raised concerns regarding improper burden shifting after an FTC Identity Theft Report had already been submitted. 

The continued reporting of these accounts has caused significant financial harm. The accounts appear as serious derogatory items on my credit reports and create the impression that I incurred debt and failed to repay it. As a result, my credit profile has been negatively affected, my credit scores have been reduced, and my ability to obtain favorable financing has been impaired. These consequences continue every month that the accounts remain on my credit reports. 

I also dispute the associated late payment histories reported in connection with these accounts. The late payments are derived from accounts that I do not recognize and did not authorize. If the accounts themselves are fraudulent or the result of identity theft, then the late payment histories associated with them are likewise inaccurate and should not continue appearing on my credit reports.

The prior complaint specifically raised concerns regarding duplicate and inconsistent reporting and requested explanations regarding why the accounts continued to appear despite active disputes. If Navy Federal Credit Union can not provide such evidence, then the accounts should be deleted immediately. 

I also request removal of all associated derogatory information, including charge-off notations, collection reporting, 30-day late payments, 60-day late payments, 90-day late payments, and any other negative account history associated with the disputed accounts. Because I do not own these accounts and filed an FTC Identity Theft Report, the continued reporting of this information is inaccurate and harmful. 

I have acted in good faith throughout this process. I reviewed my credit reports, identified accounts that I did not recognize, filed an FTC Identity Theft Report, submitted disputes, responded to requests for information, and repeatedly requested proof of ownership. Despite these efforts, Navy Federal Credit Union continues reporting the disputed accounts without providing the evidence necessary to establish that they belong to me. 

For these reasons, I respectfully request that the CFPB require Navy Federal Credit Union to conduct a complete identity theft investigation, provide all supporting documentation relied upon in its determinations, and remove all accounts and derogatory information that can not be proven to belong to me. Despite the absence of adequate validation and despite my express written dispute, the Respondent continued its collection and/or reporting activity.

III. VIOLATIONS OF THE FAIR DEBT COLLECTION PRACTICES ACT ( FDCPA ) The Respondent 's conduct constitutes one or more violations of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, 15 U.S.C. 1692 et seq. Midland Credit Management , Inc. ( " Midland Credit '' ) has attempted to collect from me on four consumer accounts ( MCM # XXXX, # XXXX, # XXXX, and # XXXX ) while sending me written correspondence that does not comply with the licensing-disclosure requirements imposed on collection agencies in North Carolina , the State where I reside and where the collection activity is directed. Midland Credit has now confirmed this non-compliance in writing to a federal regulator and continues to furnish information about these accounts to the three major consumer reporting agencies. 
I have previously raised related issues through CFPB Case # XXXX and NC DOJ XXXX XXXX. XXXX. Midland Credits response letters of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  do not address the federal violations described below. I am filing this complaint to place those federal violations directly before the Bureau. 
Issue 1 Federal violations arising from collection correspondence that omits required state licensing disclosure ( 15 U.S.C. 1692e ( 5 ), 1692e ( 10 ), and 1692f ) North Carolina law requires that " [ a ] ll collection agencies licensed under this statute doing business of a collection agency in this State, shall in all correspondence with debtors use stationery or forms which contain the permit number and the true name and address of such collection agency. '' XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX. The North Carolina Department of Insurance ( " NCDOI '' ) administers this Article and issues the collection-agency permits to which XXXX refers. 
Midland Credits XXXX XXXX XXXX letter ( to NC DOJ regarding File No. XXXX ) and XXXX XXXX XXXX letter ( to the CFPB regarding Case # XXXX ) both expressly state, " This communication is from a debt collector. '' Both letters were sent to me as the consumer. Neither letter, from Midland Credit, contains a North Carolina collection agency permit number on the stationery or anywhere in the body of the correspondence. 
When I raised this issue in my prior CFPB complaint, Midland Credits XXXX XXXX XXXX response declined to provide the permit number. It stated only that the company is " licensed and/or bonded in every state which requires such licensing and/or bonding for collection companies '' and instructed me to " contact your local state office for more information regarding licensing requirements. '' Midland Credit has now affirmatively, in writing, both ( a ) confirmed that its correspondence with me does not contain the disclosure required by XXXX, and ( b ) declined to bring the correspondence into compliance. 
I am not asking the Bureau to enforce N.C. Gen. Stat. XXXX directly. I am identifying federal violations that arise from this conduct : Violation of 15 U.S.C. 1692e and 1692e ( 10 ) false representation or deceptive means. 
By sending collection correspondence to me that holds itself out as the work of a duly licensed collection agency while omitting the statutorily required permit number, Midland Credit uses deceptive means to create the appearance of regulatory legitimacy that the correspondence itself, on its face, does not establish. Courts have recognized that a debt collectors failure to comply with state licensing-related disclosure requirements, where the collector nonetheless communicates with the consumer as a licensed entity, can constitute a 1692e violation. The Bureaus own Regulation F preamble and supervisory guidance treat state licensing compliance as a foundational element of lawful debt collection practice. 
Violation of 15 U.S.C. 1692e ( 5 ) threats to take action that can not legally be taken. 
Midland Credits XXXX XXXX XXXX letter affirmatively states that " account nos. XXXX and XXXX had been determined to be eligible for legal efforts '' and that " non-payment on the accounts may result in the accounts being forwarded to a law firm in [ my ] area to review for possible legal efforts to collect the balance. '' A debt collector that is operating in non-compliance with state licensing-disclosure requirements is not in a position to make such representations, and using the threat of legal action while simultaneously refusing to provide the state-required licensing disclosure violates 1692e ( 5 ).

Violation of 15 U.S.C. 1692f unfair or unconscionable means. 
Continuing to attempt to collect a debt, and continuing to furnish information about that debt to consumer reporting agencies, while operating in admitted non-compliance with the states correspondence-disclosure requirements, is an unfair means of collection within the meaning of 1692f. The consumer is denied the ability to verify, on the face of the correspondence, that the entity demanding payment is operating within the regulatory framework that authorizes it to do so.

Issue 2 Additional context : third-party disclosure through email subject lines ( 15 U.S.C. 1692c ( b ) ) As additional context showing a pattern of non-compliance, Midland Credit has previously sent me email collection communications with subject lines that disclose or expressly reference the existence of the debt, including " XXXX, youve got some unfinished business, '' " XXXX, Please Address Your Financial Commitment, '' " XXXX, Accept Your Low Payment Option, '' and similar formulations. Email subject lines are visible in lock-screen notifications, notification previews, and on shared or monitored devices without the message being opened. Midland Credits response to this issue in my prior CFPB complaint stated only that the subject lines were " reviewed and approved '' by its legal team and that the company " does not have control over an individual users settings on devices, applications, or email service providers. '' That response did not address the substance of the 1692c ( b ) concern. I have retained dated copies and screenshots of these communications and will produce them on request. I raise this here primarily as evidence of a broader pattern of treating consumer-facing compliance obligations as discretionary. 
What Midland Credits prior responses do not establish They do not provide a North Carolina collection agency permit number on the correspondence. 
They do not deny that the correspondence omits the permit number. 
They affirmatively decline to bring future correspondence into compliance, instead instructing me to contact a state office. 
They do not substantively address the 1692c ( b ) subject-line concern.

They do not provide documentation of the source of, or consent associated with, the email address used to contact me, as called for under the email procedures of 12 C.F.R. 1006.6 ( d ) ( 4 ).

Parallel filings I have filed a separate complaint with the NC Department of Insurance regarding the XXXX issue and a written dispute and notice-of-violation letter directly with Midland Credit by certified mail XXXX This CFPB complaint addresses the federal-law violations arising from the same underlying conduct. 
Fair Resolution ( " What would be a fair resolution? '' field ) I am requesting that Midland Credit Management , Inc. : 1. Delete the tradelines for MCM accounts # XXXX, # XXXX, # XXXX, and # XXXX from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, as a remedy for the federal violations described above, and confirm deletion in writing. A debt collector that has communicated with me in non-compliance with the state licensing-disclosure law, and has affirmatively declined to come into compliance after notice, should not be furnishing information about the collection effort to consumer reporting agencies. 
2. Identify, on the response itself, Midland Credits North Carolina collection agency permit number, and confirm in writing that all future correspondence with North Carolina debtors will include the permit number as required by XXXX. 
3. Provide a substantive written response to the 1692e, 1692e ( 5 ), 1692e ( 10 ), and 1692f issues identified above not a reference back to prior correspondence.

4. Provide documentation showing the source from which Midland Credit obtained the email address used to contact me, and the consent ( or original creditors permissible transfer of consent under 12 C.F.R. 1006.6 ( d ) ( 4 ) ) authorizing electronic communications regarding these accounts.

5. Confirm that the email address previously used for collection communications has been removed from all systems and will not be re-enrolled. 
I am not requesting that the Bureau adjudicate the underlying debts, and I acknowledge that account no. XXXX was previously recalled by the seller and is not at issue. Because this account is being furnished to the consumer reporting agencies, Resurgent/LVNV also has obligations under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. If this account can not be verified as accurate, complete, and legally reportable, it should not continue to be furnished as a valid collection account.

of notice by creditor If a creditor, within sixty days after having transmitted to an obligor a statement of the obligors account in connection with an extension of consumer credit, receives at the address disclosed under section 1637 ( b ) ( 10 ) of this title a written notice ( other than notice on a payment stub or other payment medium supplied by the creditor if the creditor so stipulates with the disclosure required under section 1637 ( a ) ( 7 ) of this title ) from the obligor in which the obligor ( 1 ) sets forth or otherwise enables the creditor to identify the name and account number ( if any ) of the obligor, ( 2 ) indicates the obligors belief that the statement contains a billing error and the amount of such billing error, and ( 3 ) sets forth the reasons for the obligors belief ( to the extent applicable ) that the statement contains a billing error, the creditor shall, unless the obligor has, after giving such written notice and before the expiration of the time limits herein specified, agreed that the statement was correct ( A ) not later than thirty days after the receipt of the notice, send a written acknowledgment thereof to the obligor, unless the action required in subparagraph ( B ) is taken within such thirty-day period, and ( B ) not later than two complete billing cycles of the creditor ( in no event later than ninety days ) after the receipt of the notice and prior to taking any action to collect the amount, or any part thereof, indicated by the obligor under paragraph ( 2 ) either ( i ) make appropriate corrections in the account of the obligor, including the crediting of any finance charges on amounts erroneously billed, and transmit to the obligor a notification of such corrections and the creditors explanation of any change in the amount indicated by the obligor under paragraph ( 2 ) and, if any such change is made and the obligor so requests, copies of documentary evidence of the obligors indebtedness ; or ( ii ) send a written explanation or clarification to the obligor, after having conducted an investigation, setting forth to the extent applicable the reasons why the creditor believes the account of the obligor was correctly shown in the statement and, upon request of the obligor, provide copies of documentary evidence of the obligors indebtedness. In the case of a billing error where the obligor alleges that the creditors billing statement reflects goods not delivered to the obligor or his designee in accordance with the agreement made at the time of the transaction, a creditor may not construe such amount to be correctly shown unless he determines that such goods were actually delivered, mailed, or otherwise sent to the obligor and provides the obligor with a statement of such determination.

After complying with the provisions of this subsection with respect to an alleged billing error, a creditor has no further responsibility under this section if the obligor continues to make substantially the same allegation with respect to such error.

( b ) Billing error For the purpose of this section, a billing error consists of any of the following : ( 1 ) A reflection on a statement of an extension of credit which was not made to the obligor or, if made, was not in the amount reflected on such statement.

( 2 ) A reflection on a statement of an extension of credit for which the obligor requests additional clarification including documentary evidence thereof.

( 3 ) A reflection on a statement of goods or services not accepted by the obligor or his designee or not delivered to the obligor or his designee in accordance with the agreement made at the time of a transaction. ( 4 ) The creditors failure to reflect properly on a statement a payment made by
the obligor or a credit issued to the obligor.

( 5 ) A computation error or similar error of an accounting nature of the creditor on a statement.

( 6 ) Failure to transmit the statement required under section 1637 ( b ) of this title to the last address of the obligor which has been disclosed to the creditor, unless that address was furnished less than twenty days before the end of the billing
cycle for which the statement is required.

( 7 ) Any other error described in regulations of the Bureau.

( c ) Action by creditor to collect amount or any part thereof regarded by obligor to be a billing error For the purposes of this section, action to collect the amount, or any part thereof, indicated by an obligor under paragraph ( 2 ) does not include the sending of statements of account, which may include finance charges on amounts in dispute, to the obligor following written notice from the obligor as specified under subsection ( a ), if ( 1 ) the obligors account is not restricted or closed because of the failure of the obligor to pay the amount indicated under paragraph ( 2 ) of subsection ( a ), and ( 2 ) the creditor indicates the payment of such amount is not required pending the creditors compliance with this section. 
Nothing in this section shall be construed to prohibit any action by a creditor to collect any amount which has not been indicated by the obligor to contain a billing error. 
( d ) Restricting or closing by creditor of account regarded by obligor to contain a billing error Pursuant to regulations of the Bureau, a creditor operating an open end consumer credit plan may not, prior to the sending of the written explanation or clarification required under paragraph ( B ) ( ii ), restrict or close an account with respect to which the obligor has indicated pursuant to subsection ( a ) that he believes such account to contain a billing error solely because of the obligors failure to pay the amount indicated to be in error. Nothing in this subsection shall be deemed to prohibit a creditor from applying against the credit limit on the obligors account the amount indicated to be in error.

( e ) Effect of noncompliance with requirements by creditor Any creditor who fails to comply with the requirements of this section or section 1666a of this title forfeits any right to collect from the obligor the amount indicated by the obligor under paragraph ( 2 ) of subsection ( a ) of this section, and any finance charges thereon, except that the amount required to be forfeited under this subsection may not exceed {$50.00}.

VIOLATION 1  Section 1692g(a)(2) failure to identify the current creditor

Johnson Mark's XX/XX/XXXXdemand letter and its XX/XX/XXXX validation cover letter both reference "our client" without unambiguously identifying the creditor to whom the alleged debt is currently owed in the cover letter itself. 15 U.S.C.  1692g(a)(2) requires identification of "the name of the creditor to whom the debt is owed." The core of this argument rests on the internal contradictions between Sunlights legal assertions and the actual language of their contracts regarding the nature of the collateral and the security interest.

Argument : Fraudulent Misrepresentation of Security Interest and Loan Characterization 1. Contradictory Definitions of Collateral In Exhibit A, Sunlight Financial explicitly denies that they hold a security interest in the consumers principal dwelling. They state that the loan is " defined and treated as personal property '' and that no " encumbrance has been placed on the residence. '' However, Exhibit C-1 directly contradicts this. The contract language states that Sunlight may make a " fixture filing '' and, crucially, that they may " enforce rights in the Equipment ... under state real estate or mortgage law. '' * The Misrepresentation : Sunlight can not claim the loan is " strictly limited '' to personal property ( to avoid Truth in Lending Act rescission rights ) while simultaneously reserving the right to use " mortgage law '' to enforce their interest. By claiming the interest is not real-estate related, they may be attempting to circumvent consumer protection laws ( like 12 C.F.R. 1026.23 ) that apply when a dwelling is used as collateral.

2. Misleading Characterization of the " Project '' In Exhibit C, the contract describes the transaction as a " home improvement project. '' * Standard industry and legal definitions typically treat " home improvements '' as enhancements to the real property.

By labeling it a " home improvement project '' in the disclosure but later insisting in Exhibit A that it is strictly " personal property '' ( like a refrigerator or a car ), Sunlight and XXXX XXXX XXXX are using shifting definitions to suit their legal needs while keeping the consumer in the dark about the true nature of the lien on their home.

3. Admission via " Corrective '' Action In Exhibit D, Sunlight states they have initiated the termination of the fixture filing ( UCC-3 ) " without taking any position on the legal analysis. '' The Argument : While they frame this as a resolution, it serves as evidence of an Improper Filing. If the filing were legitimate and correctly represented in the original loan agreement, there would be no reason to terminate it in response to a formal complaint.

The fact that they are removing the fixture filing suggests that the original filing was either unauthorized by the loans stated terms or was an attempt to cloud the property title without granting the consumer the legal protections ( like the right of rescission ) that come with real estate-collateralized loans.

4. Failure of Due Diligence A lender or agent is responsible for the accuracy of the disclosures provided to the borrower.

The bank allowed a " Fixture Filing '' to be executed ( which attaches to the real estate records ) while providing disclosures stating that no such interest in the residence existed.

This discrepancy between the recorded public filing and the private loan disclosures constitutes a material misrepresentation that affects the borrower 's ability to refinance or sell their home.

Where a creditor acquires, claims, or reserves rights associated with a security interest in a consumers principal dwelling, clear and accurate disclosures are required.

The failure to accurately disclose : the existence of the claimed interest, the legal effect of the fixture filing, the use of mortgage-law enforcement rights, and the true nature of the collateral constitutes a material disclosure violation.

The transaction documents : characterized the project as a home improvement project, authorized fixture filings connected to the real property, reserved enforcement rights under mortgage law, yet simultaneously attempted to characterize the transaction as unrelated to the residence.

This shifting characterization materially impaired the borrowers ability to : understand the true nature of the loan, understand the legal effect of the claimed lien, evaluate rescission rights, assess the impact on title to the residence, understand the implications for refinancing or sale of the property, Summary : Sunlight Financial engaged in Misrepresentation by Omission and Contradiction. I previously filed a CFPB complaint against LVNV Funding LLC / Resurgent Capital Services concerning two separate accounts ( Resurgent Account ID XXXX, acct ending in XXXX ; Resurgent Account ID XXXX, acct ending in XXXX ) for the same pattern of conduct described below. That complaint was filed on XX/XX/year> ( please cross-reference with the case number assigned by the Bureau at the time of filing ). The XXXX account is the subject of this separate complaint because Resurgents initial communication for XXXX was sent at XXXX PM on XX/XX/year> the same day the prior complaint was filed and could not be added to that earlier complaint after submission. I am filing this separate complaint to put the XXXX violations on the regulatory record promptly, before further harm to my credit occurs through furnishing of an additional tradeline. 

Issue 1 Failure to deliver a complete validation notice ( 15 U.S.C. 1692g ( a ) ; 12 C.F.R. 1006.34 ) On Thursday, XX/XX/year> at XXXX PM, Resurgent sent me an email with the subject " XXXX, info regarding acct XXXX : owned by LVNV Funding LLC, '' from sender " XXXX '' at XXXX. This is the initial communication from Resurgent regarding the XXXX account. I have received no other communications from Resurgent or LVNV regarding this account.

FDCPA 1692g ( a ) requires ( 1 ) a statement that unless the consumer disputes the validity of the debt within 30 days, the debt will be assumed valid ; ( 2 ) a statement that if the consumer notifies the debt collector in writing within the 30-day period that the debt is disputed, the debt collector will obtain verification and mail it to the consumer; and ( 3 ) a statement that on the consumers written request within the 30-day period, the debt collector will provide the name and address of the original creditor if different from the current creditor. Regulation F, 12 C.F.R. 1006.34, further requires specific itemization ( itemization date, principal at itemization, interest, fees, payments, credits ) and a standardized consumer response framework.

Issue 2 Third-party disclosure through email subject line ( 15 U.S.C. 1692c ( b ) ) The subject line of the XX/XX/year> email " XXXX, info regarding acct XXXX : owned by LVNV Funding LLC '' expressly identifies LVNV Funding LLC, a known debt-buying entity, in plain text, and references an " acct '' ( account ) " owned by '' that entity. Email subject lines are visible in mobile lock-screen previews, notification banners, shared and household devices, employer-monitored email systems, and inbox listings displayed to anyone with access to the screen. The subject line therefore communicates to any third party who sees the notification that the recipient has an account that has been sold to a debt-buying entity, in violation of 1692c ( b ).

Issue 3 Information conditioned on portal authentication does not satisfy delivery requirements The omitted content described in Issue 1 ( 30-day dispute rights, Reg F itemization, consumer response framework ) is not provided in the email and is, at most, available through the " Login '' or " View Your Account '' portal links. To the extent Resurgent will assert that the omitted validation information is made available through portal authentication, that does not satisfy the FDCPA. Section 1692g ( a ) requires the debt collector to " send the consumer a written notice. '' Making the required statutory disclosures conditionally available through portal authentication is not delivery ; it is at most an offer to provide the disclosures upon the consumers further action. The Bureaus Regulation F preamble treats validation as something the debt collector must provide, not something the consumer must retrieve through portal registration or authentication. Requiring consumers to log into a debt collectors portal as a condition of receiving statutorily-required disclosures inverts the burden the FDCPA places on debt collectors.

Issue 4 Pattern evidence across multiple accounts The XX/XX/year> email for the XXXX account is structurally similar to Resurgents initial-communication emails for XXXX prior accounts ( XXXX sent XX/XX/year> ; XXXX sent XX/XX/year> ), which are the subject of my earlier CFPB complaint. All three initial-communication emails : Come from the same sender ( " XXXX, XXXX XXXX ). 
Use subject lines of the form " XXXX, info regarding acct XXXX [ # # # # ] : owned by LVNV Funding LLC. '' Route to a Resurgent web portal via " Login '' and " View Your Account '' links. 
Lack the 30-day dispute rights language required by 1692g ( a ) ( 3 ) ( 5 ).

Lack the Regulation F 1006.34 ( d ) consumer response framework and itemization. 
Have been followed by no mailed validation notice. 

The XXXX account also involves an original creditor ( XXXX XXXX, XXXX. ) that is the same original creditor as the XXXX account. Resurgent therefore has demonstrated capability to deliver compliant 1692g notices for XXXX XXXX accounts through its established procedures and has chosen not to do so for either XXXX XXXX account at issue. The fact that Resurgent sent another non-compliant initial communication on the same day a federal regulatory complaint about exactly this conduct was filed underscores that these practices are automated, systemic, and ongoing. 

Issue 5 Anticipated furnishing to credit reporting agencies ( 12 C.F.R. 1006.30 ( a ) ) Based on Resurgents pattern with the XXXX and XXXX accounts, I anticipate that LVNV ( with Resurgent acting as servicer ) will furnish a tradeline for the XXXX account to the major consumer reporting agencies in the coming weeks. Under 12 C.F.R. 1006.30 ( a ), a debt collector is prohibited from furnishing information about a debt to a consumer reporting agency unless the debt collector has first either ( i ) spoken with the consumer about the debt, or ( ii ) sent a written or electronic communication about the debt and waited a reasonable period to receive notice of undeliverability. To the extent Resurgent relies on the XX/XX/year> email as the predicate communication, the XXXX should consider whether a communication that itself fails to deliver the validation content required by 1692g ( a ) ( 3 ) ( 5 ) and 1006.34 ( d ) satisfies the 1006.30 ( a ) predicate requirement.

XXXX  response does not address the substance of my complaint. Instead of proving that I opened, authorized, used, benefited from, or legally owe this account, XXXX attacked the wording of my complaint by claiming it shares the same verbiage as other consumers. That statement is unsupported, irrelevant, and does not prove that this account belongs to me. 

This complaint was submitted by me, based on my credit report, my identity theft claim, and my own dispute of this specific XXXX account. XXXX has not identified any credit repair organization, third party, or fraudulent submitter. Similar legal wording does not make a complaint illegitimate. Consumers are allowed to cite the same consumer protection laws when they are harmed by the same type of conduct. 

XXXX  response also requests a police report, but XXXX does not explain why my identity theft submission and supporting documents are insufficient. An FTC Identity Theft Report is not a casual statement. The FTC explains that the Identity Theft Report is generated through XXXX, is submitted under penalty of perjury, is made available to law enforcement, and is designed to notify businesses that their records XXXX contain fraudulent information about the consumer. The FCRA definition of an identity theft report includes an official valid report filed with an appropriate federal, state, or local law enforcement agency or other government agency deemed appropriate, where false filing can carry criminal penalties. 

XXXX can not use the absence of a separate police report as a shortcut to avoid addressing the actual issue : this account is the result of identity theft, I did not authorize it, and XXXX is continuing to report or collect it. If XXXX believes a police report is legally required in addition to the FTC Identity Theft Report, XXXX should identify the exact legal basis for that position and explain why the FTC Identity Theft Report and supporting identity theft documentation are insufficient.

Those are exactly the types of identifying information that can be misused in identity theft.

Midlands response does not show a reasonable investigation into identity theft.

Under FCRA 623, 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 6 ), furnishers must have reasonable procedures to respond to identity-theft block notices from credit reporting agencies and prevent refurnishing blocked identity-theft information. If XXXX received notice through the credit bureaus that this account was identified as identity theft, XXXX had a duty to respond appropriately and not simply rely on seller data.

Any prior dispute activity should not be treated as evidence that I acknowledged, verified, accepted, or assumed responsibility for this account. It may itself be connected to the identity theft or misuse of my information.

I am filing this complaint against Midland Credit Management XXXX XXXX ( MCM ) for violations of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ), 15 U.S.C. 1692 et seq., Regulation F ( 12 C.F.R. Part 1006 ), and the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681 et seq. 

MCM sent me a collection email regarding MCM Account # XXXX, associated with an alleged original account ending in XXXX with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ), claiming I owe {$960.00}. I am a consumer as defined under 15 U.S.C. 1692a ( 3 ). This debt is disputed in its entirety.

8. FCRA FURNISHING ( 1681s-2 ( b ) ) : If MCM is reporting this account to any credit bureau , furnishing an unverified, unitemized, and disputed balance may constitute inaccurate reporting.

The XXXX URL Midland directed me to requires the consumer to ( a ) provide a Midland account number, ( b ) provide the last four digits of the consumer 's Social Security Number, AND ( c ) click through and agree to a Terms of Use ( " TOU '' ) before any account information can be accessed. The TOU includes binding arbitration, exclusive California jurisdiction, electronic communications consent, a {$100.00} liability cap, and waiver of jury trial.

3. CONDITIONING VALIDATION ON A TERMS OF USE VIOLATES FDCPA 809 ( b ). Under 15 USC 1692g ( b ), upon a written request for validation, the debt collector must cease collection until validation is mailed or otherwise provided to the consumer. Validation must be PROVIDED to the consumer unconditionally. Conditioning the provision of validation on ( a ) the consumer providing their own SSN to gain access to their own debt records, and ( b ) the consumer agreeing to an adhesion contract that includes arbitration and a {$100.00} liability cap, is not validation under 809 ( b ). It is an attempt to bind the consumer to a contract before allowing access to records the collector is statutorily required to provide.

4. THE FALSE CLAIM OF " ENCLOSED VERIFICATION '' IS ITSELF AN FDCPA 807 VIOLATION. Under 15 USC 1692e, a debt collector may not use any false, deceptive, or misleading representation in connection with the collection of a debt. Stating that verification was " enclosed for your records '' when nothing was actually enclosed is a false representation about the status of the debt and the collector 's compliance with validation requirements.

I demand this account be taken off immediately.

XXXX has failed to validate an alleged debt within thirty days of receiving a written validation request under 15 U.S.C. 1692g ( b ), while continuing to furnish the alleged debt to a consumer reporting agency and certifying it as accurate through the standard XXXX process. XXXX has also misrepresented itself as the original creditor on the disputed tradeline. 
BACKGROUND On XX/XX/year>, I sent XXXX a written debt validation request by USPS Certified Mail, tracking number XXXX, under 15 U.S.C. 1692g ( b ). The request was sent without acknowledgment of the underlying alleged debt and demanded that XXXX provide written verification of the debt, the name and address of the original creditor, and documentation of XXXX 's authority to collect. XXXX 's reported address ( XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX, XXXX, FL XXXX for collections correspondence, with the main office at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, FL XXXX ) appears on the tradeline data XXXX  discloses for this account. 
The thirty-day FDCPA validation window expired on XX/XX/year>. As of the filing date of this complaint, XXXX has not responded in any form. XXXX has provided no validation, no original-creditor identification, no documentation of its collection authority, and no acknowledgment of the validation request. 
CONTINUED COLLECTION ACTIVITY DESPITE NO VALIDATION During the period in which validation was outstanding, XXXX continued to furnish the alleged debt to Equifax and certified the debt as accurate in response to a parallel dispute filed with Equifax on XX/XX/year> ( USPS Certified Mail tracking XXXX ). On XX/XX/year>, XXXX  issued its investigation results ( Confirmation # XXXX ) stating : " Our investigation concluded that the disputed information is reporting accurately. '' XXXX had not validated the debt at any point before XX/XX/year>, and has not validated it since. XXXX 's certification of the debt as accurate through the XXXX  process, in the absence of any validation in response to my 1692g request, is itself prohibited collection activity under 1692g ( b ) and a false representation of the character and status of the debt under 1692e ( 2 ) ( A ) and 1692e ( 8 ).

MISREPRESENTATION OF ORIGINAL CREDITOR On the XXXX  tradeline data disclosed in the XX/XX/year> investigation results, XXXX lists itself as the original creditor. XXXX is a debt collection agency. XXXX is not the original creditor on this alleged debt. Listing itself as the original creditor on a consumer credit reporting tradeline is a false representation of the character or status of the debt under 15 U.S.C. 1692e ( 2 ) ( A ), a false representation of the credit information being furnished under 1692e ( 8 ), and a deceptive means of attempting to collect a debt under 1692e ( 10 ).

PARALLEL DISPUTES FILED Parallel disputes were filed with XXXX  and XXXX  concerning the same tradeline. XXXX XXXX dispute results, returned on XX/XX/year>, stated " Remains '' the tradeline was not corrected. XXXX XXXX dispute results, returned XX/XX/year>, stated the information was " reporting accurately '' and added an Additional Information field reading " Consumer Disputes This Account Information. '' The tradeline does not appear on TransUnion. 
In all three bureau interactions, XXXX had the opportunity to respond to a notice of dispute under the XXXX process and to provide validation. XXXX did neither. XXXX simply certified the tradeline as accurate without producing the validation a 1692g written request requires. 
VIOLATIONS ALLEGED Based on the facts above, XXXX appears to have violated the following provisions of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act : 15 U.S.C. 1692g ( b ) Failure to validate the alleged debt within thirty days of a written validation request, while continuing to engage in collection activity ( i.e., continuing to furnish to a consumer reporting agency and certifying the debt as accurate ).

15 U.S.C. 1692e ( 2 ) ( A ) False representation of the character, amount, or legal status of the debt, by certifying the debt as accurate through the XXXX process without producing validation, and by misrepresenting itself as the original creditor.

15 U.S.C. 1692e ( 8 ) Communicating credit information that is known or should be known to be false, by furnishing unvalidated information to a consumer reporting agency and certifying it as accurate.

15 U.S.C. 1692e ( 10 ) Use of false representations or deceptive means to collect or attempt to collect a debt, by misrepresenting itself as the original creditor on the tradeline.

Separately, under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ), XXXX is prohibited from furnishing information to a consumer reporting agency that XXXX knows or has reasonable cause to believe is inaccurate. Certifying an unvalidated debt as accurate, and reporting itself as the original creditor when it is not, appears to violate this provision as well.

I am submitting this complaint because * * Educational Credit Management Corporation ( ECMC ) * * continues to report a derogatory collection account on my consumer credit reports that I believe is inaccurate, incomplete, and has not been properly verified as required by the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ). I have exercised my rights under the FCRA by disputing the accuracy of this account and requesting that the consumer reporting agencies conduct a reasonable reinvestigation. Rather than receiving documentation establishing the accuracy of the account, I have received only generalized responses indicating that the account was " verified '' or continues to be reported as accurate. These responses do not explain what information was reviewed, what records were relied upon, or how ECMC substantiated the information being reported. A statement that an account has been verified, without supporting evidence, does not satisfy the requirements of federal law.

The ECMC account is currently being reported as a * * collection account with a derogatory status * *, and its continued presence on my credit reports has caused substantial harm to my financial standing. A collection account significantly affects creditworthiness and may negatively influence decisions regarding loans, credit cards, housing, employment, and insurance. Because of the serious impact this reporting has on my financial life, I requested that ECMC and the consumer reporting agencies conduct a thorough investigation using original source documentation rather than relying on automated electronic verification systems.

Under * * 15 U.S.C. 1681i * *, when a consumer disputes information appearing on a credit report, the consumer reporting agency is required to conduct a reasonable reinvestigation to determine whether the disputed information is accurate. Likewise, under * * 15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ) * *, consumer reporting agencies must maintain reasonable procedures to assure the maximum possible accuracy of the information they report. These statutory obligations require more than transmitting an electronic dispute to the furnisher and accepting an automated response. They require an investigation based upon competent documentary evidence that establishes the accuracy and completeness of the information being reported.

To date, I have not received any documentation demonstrating that ECMC possesses sufficient evidence to support the continued reporting of this collection account. I requested copies of the original promissory note or other legally binding agreement, documentation identifying me as the obligor, complete account records, payment history, account statements, records establishing the balance claimed to be owed, documentation showing the date of first delinquency, and any documents supporting the transfer or assignment of the account to ECMC if applicable. I also requested copies of the records relied upon during the investigation and an explanation of the method of verification used. Despite these requests, no competent documentary evidence has been provided.

If ECMC maintains that the account is accurate, then it should have no difficulty producing complete business records establishing its accuracy. These records should include the original signed agreement or promissory note, complete servicing history, payment ledger, records supporting the balance reported, documentation establishing the date of default, records demonstrating that the account was lawfully transferred or assigned to ECMC if it was acquired from another entity, and documentation demonstrating ECMC 's authority to report and collect the alleged debt. Without this documentation, I have no way to determine whether the information appearing on my credit reports is accurate, complete, or legally reportable.

I am also concerned that the investigation conducted by the consumer reporting agencies may have relied exclusively upon automated verification systems instead of an independent review of the underlying records. Numerous courts have recognized that a reasonable investigation under the Fair Credit Reporting Act requires more than accepting the furnisher 's computerized response when a consumer specifically disputes the accuracy of an account. A meaningful reinvestigation requires examination of the original source documents and consideration of the evidence presented by the consumer. If ECMC merely confirmed the account through an automated process without reviewing the original records, then the investigation was not reasonable within the meaning of the Fair Credit Reporting Act.

In addition, I requested disclosure of the method of verification used during the investigation. Specifically, I requested identification of the individual or department that conducted the investigation, the documents that were reviewed, the records relied upon, and the procedures used to determine that the account was accurately reported. Instead of receiving this information, I received only a conclusory statement that the account had been verified. Such a response does not provide sufficient transparency to determine whether the investigation complied with federal law.

The continued reporting of this ECMC collection account has caused ongoing damage to my consumer credit profile. Credit reports play an essential role in determining a consumer 's access to credit, housing, employment opportunities, and favorable financial terms. Because of the significant consequences associated with derogatory reporting, Congress enacted the Fair Credit Reporting Act to ensure that only information that is accurate, complete, and verifiable appears on consumer credit reports. Allowing inaccurate or unsupported information to remain on a consumer report undermines these important protections.

I am not requesting the removal of accurate information simply because it is unfavorable. Rather, I am requesting that ECMC comply with its legal obligations by substantiating the disputed information with competent documentary evidence. If ECMC possesses original business records demonstrating that every aspect of its reporting is accurate, then those records should be produced. If ECMC can not produce the original documentation necessary to verify the account, then the account should not continue to be reported as a collection account on my consumer credit reports.

If ECMC acquired servicing rights or ownership of the alleged obligation from another entity, I request copies of any assignment agreements, transfer documentation, servicing records, or other evidence establishing its legal authority to report the account. If ECMC is unable to establish its legal authority through competent evidence, then it should not continue reporting this account to the nationwide consumer reporting agencies.

I respectfully request that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau require ECMC and the consumer reporting agencies to conduct a complete and lawful reinvestigation of this disputed account. I request that ECMC provide copies of the original promissory note or agreement, complete payment history, servicing records, account statements, documentation supporting the reported balance, records establishing the date of first delinquency, documentation establishing any assignment or transfer of the account, and every document relied upon during its investigation. I also request disclosure of the method of verification used and an explanation of how ECMC concluded that the account was accurately reported.

If ECMC can not produce competent documentary evidence establishing that this collection account is accurate, complete, and legally verifiable, I request that it be permanently deleted from all of my consumer credit reports. I further request written confirmation of the investigation results, copies of all documents relied upon, and an updated copy of my consumer credit reports reflecting the deletion of any information that can not be verified in accordance with * * 15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ) and 1681i * *. My request is based solely on my right to have consumer reporting that is accurate, complete, and supported by competent evidence as required by federal law.

CFPB Rebuttal to Complaint No. XXXX I categorically reject the response submitted by Fair Collections & Outsourcing , Inc. Their response fails to validate this alleged debt and fails to establish that I entered into this lease, occupied this apartment, or am legally responsible for the alleged balance of {$12000.00}. Instead of producing competent evidence proving their claim, Fair Collections & Outsourcing submitted incomplete, contradictory, and internally inconsistent documents that raise serious questions regarding the identity of the actual tenant and the legitimacy of this account. 

The burden of proving that this debt belongs to me rests entirely with Fair Collections & Outsourcing and XXXX XXXX. That burden has not been met. Simply mailing internal account records, an unsigned ledger, and an incomplete electronic lease does not establish legal liability. 

The lease they submitted contains nothing more than an electronic DocuSign signature that they claim belongs to me. It is not my handwritten signature, and they have produced absolutely no evidence establishing that I was the individual who electronically signed the lease. 

Even more concerning is what they deliberately omitted. 

The lease packet does not include the DocuSign Certificate of Completion ( also known as the Certificate of Evidence or Signature Validation page ) that accompanies every properly executed DocuSign agreement. This is the document that authenticates an electronic signature and records the complete audit trail, including the DocuSign Envelope ID, timestamps, IP addresses, email addresses used during execution, authentication methods, device information, and every action taken during the signing process. 

Without the Certificate of Completion, there is no way to determine : Who actually signed the lease. 
What email address was used. 
What IP address the document was signed from. 
What device was used. 
Whether any identity verification occurred. 
Whether the signer successfully authenticated their identity. 
Whether the electronic signature is even attributable to me. 

An electronic signature page, standing alone, proves absolutely nothing. It is merely an image of a signature without the audit trail required to authenticate it. If XXXX XXXX  genuinely possesses a valid electronically executed lease, then producing the complete DocuSign audit trail should be effortless. Their failure to produce the very document that validates the electronic signature is a glaring omission that completely undermines the reliability of the lease they rely upon. 

The financial records they submitted create even more doubt. 

Their own resident ledger reflects multiple credit card payments for application fees, deposits, rent, and move-in costs. Every one of those payments was later reversed or returned, and the ledger specifically identifies the payment method as an " unauthorized '' credit card. 

That raises an obvious question : Whose credit card was it? 

Every electronic credit card transaction generates payment processing records. XXXX XXXX  should possess transaction records, authorization attempts, reversal or chargeback information, merchant processing records, and documentation identifying the cardholder or the individual who attempted to use that payment method. 

If the card was determined to be unauthorized, then who owned it? 

What name was associated with it? 

What billing address was used? 

What fraud investigation was conducted? 

Where are those records? 

None of this information has been produced. 

The ledger also reflects subsequent payments identified by payment numbers that appear to correspond to checks, money orders, cashier 's checks, or another negotiable payment instrument. Regardless of the payment type, those instruments are traceable through the issuing financial institution or payment provider. 

Again, the obvious question is : Who purchased or issued those payment instruments? 

If XXXX XXXX accepted those payments, then it either knows or can determine who tendered those funds. If those payments were dishonored or became part of the alleged balance, there should be documentation identifying the purchaser, remitter, account holder, or other identifying information associated with those transactions. 

Instead of identifying the individual who actually made those payments, Fair Collections & Outsourcing has simply attempted to assign liability to me without producing a single document connecting me to those payment instruments. 

Those payment records are among the strongest evidence available to identify the individual who actually rented this apartment. Fair Collections & Outsourcing ignored that evidence and instead chose to pursue me without first identifying the person who actually conducted these transactions. 

That is not debt validation. 

That is not a reasonable investigation. 

Their own accounting records further contradict their claim. 

Throughout the resident ledger are repeated entries labeled " XXXX XXXX XXXX '' and " XXXX XXXX XXXX. '' Vacant. 

Their own records repeatedly classify the apartment as vacant. 

If the apartment was vacant, then who was occupying it? 

How can XXXX XXXX simultaneously claim that I resided in the apartment while charging vacant utility recovery? 

Their own business records directly contradict their allegation that I was ever a resident. 

The reporting history is equally inconsistent. 

The original tradeline under XXXX XXXX  Lofts 590 reports : Opened : XX/XX/XXXX Closed : XX/XX/XXXX Reported : XX/XX/XXXX Status : Account submitted to collection / Account transferred However, a second collection later appears under Fair Collections & Outsourcing , Inc., reporting : Opened : XX/XX/XXXX Collection account : XX/XX/XXXX First reported to the credit bureaus : XX/XX/XXXX Balance : {$12000.00} Status : Unpaid account disputed ; Account submitted to collection Term : One month Months reviewed : 31 These dates are inconsistent and unexplained. 

According to XXXX XXXX 's own records, this account allegedly closed in XX/XX/XXXX. If that is true, why did Fair Collections & Outsourcing wait until XXXX XXXXnearly three years laterto begin reporting this collection to the consumer reporting agencies? 

Why was the account dormant for years before suddenly appearing as a newly reported collection? 

No explanation has been provided. 

This reporting history raises serious questions regarding the accuracy and handling of this account and further undermines the reliability of the information being furnished. 

Most importantly, Fair Collections & Outsourcing has failed to produce a single piece of objective evidence establishing that I was ever physically present at this property. 

I have never lived at XXXX XXXX XXXX South, Apartment XXXX, XXXX, Virginia. 

I have never occupied this apartment. 

I have never received keys. 

I have never moved into this property. 

I have never entered into a lease agreement with XXXX XXXX. 

Despite attempting to collect nearly {$13000.00} from me, neither XXXX Collections & XXXX nor XXXX XXXX has produced : A government-issued photo identification presented during the leasing process. 
The verified rental application bearing my signature. 
The complete XXXX XXXX of XXXX. 
Identity verification records. 
The electronic XXXX XXXX. 
Leasing office surveillance.

Key issuance records.

Building access logs.

Parking registration.

Utility accounts in my name.

Renters insurance records.

Move-in inspection documents signed by me.

Package delivery records.

Any evidence placing me at this property. 

Apartment communities routinely require applicants to present government-issued photo identification before possession of an apartment is granted. If XXXX XXXX followed its own leasing procedures, then it should have retained documentation identifying the individual to whom it rented this apartment. 

Accordingly, I request that Fair Collections & Outsourcing and Equity Residential produce : The government-issued photo identification presented during leasing. 
The complete DocuSign Certificate of Completion and audit trail. 
All electronic signature authentication logs. 
IP addresses and device information associated with the lease execution. 
The rental application. 
Payment processor records identifying the owner of the unauthorized credit card. 
Documentation identifying the purchaser or issuer of the subsequent payment instruments. 
Any fraud investigation conducted after the payment methods were determined to be unauthorized or returned. 
Any documentation demonstrating that I personally occupied or took possession of Apartment XXXX. 

If they can not produce this evidence, then they can not establish that I was the tenant. 

What makes this matter even more troubling is that this is not the only apartment-related collection that has recently appeared on my credit reports for properties where I have never lived. Multiple rental collections from unrelated apartment communities have appeared despite the fact that I have never resided at those locations. This pattern raises significant concerns that my personal information may have been used by another individual. Regardless of the cause, Fair Collections & Outsourcing has made no meaningful effort to determine who actually incurred this debt before attempting to collect it from me.

Fair Collections & Outsourcing has failed to validate this account. Their response consists of incomplete records, contradictory dates, missing identity verification, an incomplete DocuSign lease lacking its required audit trail, unauthorized payment methods with no explanation as to who used them, traceable payment instruments they failed to investigate, and absolutely no competent evidence establishing that I entered into this lease or occupied this apartment. 

The evidence they submitted does not prove their case. It raises more questions than answers. 

I therefore request that the CFPB require Fair Collections & Outsourcing and Equity Residential to either produce competent evidence establishing that I personally entered into this lease and incurred this obligation or immediately instruct them to delete this account from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. 

I further request that all collection activity cease until competent evidence of my identity and legal liability is produced. 

This debt is not mine. I have never lived at this property, and after being given the opportunity to validate this account, Fair Collections & Outsourcing has failed to produce evidence sufficient to establish that I am the individual responsible. The continued reporting and collection of this account without competent proof of identity and liability is inaccurate and continues to cause substantial harm to my credit profile. I respectfully request that this matter be resolved by ordering the immediate deletion of this collection from all consumer reporting agencies.

The continued reporting of this account affects my ability to obtain credit, qualify for favorable interest rates, secure housing, and pursue other financial opportunities. Because of these serious consequences, I requested that Diversified Adjustment Service conduct a complete investigation supported by original business records rather than relying solely upon automated verification systems or electronic responses.

Under * * 15 U.S.C. 1681i * *, once a consumer disputes the accuracy of information appearing on a credit report, the consumer reporting agency must conduct a reasonable reinvestigation to determine whether the disputed information is accurate. Likewise, * * 15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ) * * requires consumer reporting agencies to maintain reasonable procedures to assure the maximum possible accuracy of the information they report. These statutory obligations require more than forwarding a dispute electronically and accepting a computerized response from the furnisher. A reasonable investigation requires review of competent documentary evidence establishing that the disputed information is accurate, complete, and legally reportable.

Because Diversified Adjustment Service is a third-party debt collector, I requested documentation establishing that it has the legal authority to collect and report the alleged debt.
